text: So a rain gauge is a simple thing, you just catch rain in a funnel and let it drain down into a tube. That tube is a cylinder and it's got a scale down the side. The top is always wider than the tube, that's very deliberate. You're magnifying the measurement. So if the top area is ten times the area of the tube, then one inch of rain will fill up the tube to ten inches. So it's easy to measure, very accurately, hundredths of an inch. But there's problems with rain gauges. First, you've got evaporation. It's very easy for water to evaporate from it, particularly in warm weather or windy weather, and it'll evaporate very quickly. So it's just not really measuring correctly. And the other big problem is wind. If you've got strong winds, the turbulence around the mouth of the gauge will blow rain over the top, so it'll underestimate the rainfall.
